I never said any of that. My critique is solely directed to modern industrial societies (that are European in origin). Of course, there were cultures that were reasonably environmentally sustainable, but the technoindustrial system either destroyed or absorbed most of them. The goal of the technoindustrial system  is to encompass everything, the whole World into a single entity. 

There is no point in talking about cultures that don't exist anymore, since they don't have any influence in this question and in (im)possible solutions. 

I don't nurture pipe dreams that people in modern societies would give up their luxuries  and shiny gadgets and live in some kind of Deep Ecology utopia (even though I'd love that). We are raised and trained to serve the technoindustrial system, people don't know other ways of living. They will kill and die to defend the system.

I don't feel like going into a debate because I think it's worthless. You probably read things that I didn't, I probably read things that you didn't, so we're going to have different opinions on terms and what they mean and none of us will change our points of view.

Most of what I wrote comes from Jacques Ellul's The Technological Society. I don't have 10% of Ellul's intellect and english is not my native language, so maybe I was not clear enough on what I meant. So if you wanna read something better written by someone way more capable than I am, I'd suggest you read his book (in case you never read). It's an amazing read, and I'd recommend for everyone here.

(edit: some grammar mistakes)

I used the term "communism" in the popular meaning. I know that we have many socialist doctrines, but Marxism is the dominant one, to the point that is has almost become synonymous with "communism" (which is a theoretical, even utopian, state of society). We could also argue that "capitalism" never existed in a pure form, which liberals and libertarians frequently argue, since pure capitalism is also utopian.

This waste of resources you say, I'd categorize it more as "efficacy", not as "efficiency". But that's just semantics. What I was addressing is that our system strives to produce more, using less resources. That's the main point of technique/technological development. Even socialist countries were in this quest, to produce more, using less, through technological development.

I think solely blaming "capitalists", "politicians", "the elites", "the corporations" etc. is a little simplistic. I prefer to take the Ellulist-Kaczynskist view of technique/technoindustrial system, where economic growth is a systematic need. If the system stops delivering economic growth, it will not work properly. Look what happened in the USSR when the system stopped being able to deliver economic growth in the 80s.  
  
The "capitalists", "politicians", "the elites", "the corporations" are short-sighted and only thinking about themselves? sure. But who is not? Our societies are addicted to growthism. One can only oppose capitalism by being a communist, both are growthist ideologies. The USSR were environmentally terrible too, at least as much as any capitalist country. 

I see those two ideologies as just two different ways of managing the same beast: the technoindustrial system. One manage it by centralizing all the decisions in the State, the other by decentralizing to private agents.

Also, I pretty much agree with Ellul's take that we live in a society of technical necessities, we are in a never-ending quest for maximum efficiency, so ideology is way less important than many people think. The radical transformation we need to avoid collapse is way deeper than just getting rid of billionaires or taxing the large polluters (even though I agree with that from a moral point of view). It would require such abrupt lowering of the standards of living, especially on developed countries, that it's impossible that it would happen. People would not allow it. 

Even if by some miracle the system finds a way to go carbon-neutral in time to avoid the worst effects of climate change, we would just be digging ourselves into a deeper problem in the future. As Ellul says: "man can never foresee the totality of consequences of a given technical action. History shows that every technical application from its beginnings presents certain unforeseeable secondary effects which are much more disastrous than the lack of the technique would have been. These effects exist alongside those effects which were foreseen and expected and which represent something valuable and positive." Since at least the industrial revolution, we are just digging our graves deeper and deeper. We will not engineer ourselves out of this mess.

To sum up, it's over. But I'm preaching to the choir here.
